# Bootstrapping the Architecture 2.0 Ecosystem {#sec-bootstrapping-ecosystem}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"Organizing complexity through shared design rules and standard abstractions allowed an entire generation of engineers to build systems of unprecedented scale."*
>
> — Carver Mead and Lynn Conway, *Introduction to VLSI Systems* (1980) [@MeadConway1980VLSI]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note.** Carver Mead and Lynn Conway transformed semiconductor design by establishing scalable abstractions and shared design rules that decoupled logic design from fabrication physics. In Architecture 2.0, our challenge is to create open schemas, open signoff stacks, neutral benchmark rules, and competitive grand challenges that decouple autonomous search loops from proprietary CAD lock-in.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
How do we coordinate open data standards, open PDK signoff stacks, neutral consortium benchmarks, and competitive grand challenges to transform AI-assisted hardware exploration into a trusted, auditable engineering discipline across our industry?
:::

Building an enterprise-grade ecosystem for autonomous computer architecture requires us to coordinate action across industry, academia, standards bodies, and tooling vendors. In Architecture 1.0, microarchitectural exploration relied on hand-crafted Hardware Description Language (HDL) modules, manual design space sweeps, and monolithic Electronic Design Automation (EDA) licenses. In Architecture 2.0, autonomous search loops and generative models explore vast design spaces dynamically. Just as VLSI co-design, deep learning benchmarking, and open instruction set architectures required shared foundations, our discipline demands open data standards, open signoff harnesses, neutral governance, and competitive grand challenges to transform AI-assisted hardware exploration into an auditable engineering discipline.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, we achieve four core objectives.

- **Sequence** the six master staging steps required to construct an open Architecture 2.0 ecosystem.
- **Formulate** open schema protocols and cryptographic attempt lineage headers ($s_{\text{design}}, s_{\text{env}}$).
- **Establish** neutral consortium benchmark governance and public failure repository indexing.
- **Deploy** living web hub resources and containerized starter kits at [arch2.mlsysbook.ai](https://arch2.mlsysbook.ai).
:::

## Ecosystem Staging and Execution Sequence {#sec-staging-sequence}

When we deploy autonomous search loops into hardware design without shared infrastructure, we risk compounding chaos rather than accelerating progress. Building a resilient engineering ecosystem demands that we carefully stage our investments, ensuring that foundational data schemas and physical signoff harnesses precede the deployment of generative models or unconstrained design space exploration.

In @tbl-ecosystem-staging-sequence, we summarize the six sequential steps required to construct this engineering infrastructure across three primary columns: the step sequence index, the core ecosystem action, and the resulting primary deliverable. The table highlights how foundational schemas and physical signoff harnesses anchor the early steps before our discipline advances to consortium governance, grand challenges, public failure repositories, and workforce badging.

| **Step** | **Ecosystem action** | **Primary deliverable** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Step 1** | **Shared Data Schemas and Tool Contracts** | Open schemas for prompt logs, tool flags, ASTs, CDFGs, and container execution environments |
| **Step 2** | **Open PDKs and Cloud Silicon Shuttles** | Open PDK access (Sky130/ASAP7) and cloud shuttle passes with OpenROAD/OpenSTA physical signoff telemetry |
| **Step 3** | **Consortium Governance and Matched Benchmarks** | MLCommons-style working groups enforcing closed and open benchmark divisions across XR, CXL, and UCIe targets |
| **Step 4** | **Grand Challenges and Architecture Contests** | Annual competitions at ISCA, MICRO, and DAC focused on timing closure, PPA optimization, and formal verification |
| **Step 5** | **Public Repositories of Failed Attempts** | Shared logs of unroutable layouts, negative slack, UPF domain conflicts, and synthesis failures |
| **Step 6** | **University Curricula and Conference Badges** | Cross-disciplinary university training and Autonomous Workflow Certified (AWC) badges |

: **Staging Sequence for Ecosystem Bootstrapping.** We must execute ecosystem investments in sequence to guarantee that foundational schemas and signoff harnesses exist before deploying autonomous search or generation tools. {#tbl-ecosystem-staging-sequence}

When we trace this progression from Step 1 through Step 6, the initial two steps establish the pre-competitive physical substrate that makes reproducible exploration possible. Step 3 and Step 4 provide the consortium governance structures and competitive targets needed to align industrial and academic research teams. Step 5 and Step 6 complete the ecosystem by institutionalizing knowledge from failed design attempts and certifying workforce competencies.

Following this progression guarantees that each technological advance builds upon verifiable, decision-critical evidence.

## Shared Data Schemas and Tool Contracts {#sec-standardized-data-lineage}

The first step of our execution sequence addresses the root cause of fragmentation in modern AI-assisted design, which stems from a lack of interoperable data contracts. Today, our engineering teams often rely on custom JSON or YAML formats to record prompt sequences, simulator outputs, and physical layout metrics. Consequently, machine learning models trained in one environment fail to generalize when we transfer them to a different CAD flow or target technology node. When we release neutral, open specifications for decision contexts, attempt vectors, and tool execution logs, we enable cross-organizational knowledge transfer without exposing proprietary intellectual property.

To resolve this fragmentation, we look to how Accellera and IEEE 1666 (SystemC, an open system-level modeling standard based on C++) bootstrapped system-level modeling by releasing an open-source C++ reference implementation before commercial EDA vendors built proprietary tools around it [@IEEE2011SystemC1666]. We must standardize an *Open Agentic Interface* (OAI) across three core schemas:

1. **Design Problem Formulations.** Explicit declarations of swept parameters, locked constraints, evaluation checks, and acceptance criteria. For example, in a mobile XR spatial accelerator exploration loop (@sec-architecture-20-ontology), the problem formulation defines architectural search bounds (such as PE array sizes $16\times16$ to $64\times64$ and SRAM capacity $256\text{ KB}$ to $2\text{ MB}$) and system obligations ($3\text{ W}$ Thermal Design Power limit and $120\text{ FPS}$ latency constraint). It also declares target instruction sets (such as RISC-V RV64GCV, a 64-bit open instruction set architecture featuring general-purpose and vector extensions), interconnect interfaces (such as UCIe, Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express, and CXL, Compute Express Link), and target technology nodes (such as ASAP7 $7\text{ nm}$ open PDK alongside commercial TSMC N7 and N3 nodes).
2. **Attempt Lineage Headers.** Cryptographically verifiable records linking candidate artifacts to their parent transformations, tool flags, structural representations, and environment configurations [@SLSA2026Framework]. For example, when an AI generator modifies a SystemC TLM memory controller or synthesizes an HLS C++ kernel (@sec-data-representations-world-models), the lineage header records a cryptographic hash of the input prompt, parent git commit, Abstract Syntax Tree (AST), Control-Data Flow Graph (CDFG), MLIR/CIRCT Intermediate Representation (IR), container image digest (`docker://arch2/tools@sha256:...`), random seed, UPF (Unified Power Format, IEEE 1801 standard for specifying low-power design intent) power state declarations, and CLI arguments.
3. **Multi-Fidelity Environmental Contracts and Tool AI-Readiness Certification.** Typed schemas specifying input prerequisites, output guarantees, and error bounds across analytical models, cycle-level simulators, and RTL synthesis tools. Certifying simulators and EDA engines (such as gem5, Verilator, SCALE-Sim, Ramulator, OpenROAD, Yosys, and OpenSTA) as "AI-ready" ensures they expose deterministic container APIs, structured JSON-LD/protobuf state exports, fine-grained checkpoint recovery, and machine-parsable error channels required for autonomous agent loops (@sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces).

To operationalize these three core schemas across our discipline, we standardize their implementation through the Open Agentic Interface. In @fig-oai-schemas, we illustrate how the OAI specification structures these schemas into an auditable data pipeline. Visually, the diagram organizes the specification into three side-by-side upper components (Schema 1 Design Problem Formulation, Schema 2 Attempt Lineage Header, and Schema 3 Environmental Contract) that all converge into a foundational bottom container representing secure, cross-organizational knowledge transfer.

![**The Open Agentic Interface (OAI) standardizes three core schemas to solve data fragmentation.** Design Problem Formulations declare search bounds and TDP obligations; Attempt Lineage Headers provide SLSA cryptographic provenance linking candidates to parent tool transformations; Multi-Fidelity Environmental Contracts certify simulators and EDA tools as AI-ready execution engines. Together they enable cross-organizational knowledge transfer without exposing proprietary foundry PDK parameters or confidential RTL.](images/F12b-oai-schemas){#fig-oai-schemas width="100%" fig-alt="Diagram of the three core schemas of the Open Agentic Interface: Schema 1 Design Problem Formulation (swept bounds, TDP limit, target ISAs and nodes), Schema 2 Attempt Lineage Header (SLSA cryptographic hash, AST/CDFG representations, container image digest), and Schema 3 Environmental Contract (input preconditions, error bounds, AI-ready certified tools gem5, Verilator, OpenROAD, Yosys, OpenSTA). A pink bottom box shows cross-organizational knowledge transfer without exposing proprietary IP."}

The diagram highlights the three structural pillars of the OAI specification. Schema 1 (Design Problem Formulation) formalizes architectural search bounds, system performance obligations, and target technology nodes. Schema 2 (Attempt Lineage Header) establishes supply-chain security by attaching SLSA cryptographic hashes, container image digests, and AST/CDFG graph representations to every candidate artifact. Schema 3 (Multi-Fidelity Environmental Contract) certifies simulators and EDA engines (including gem5, Verilator, OpenROAD, Yosys, and OpenSTA) as AI-ready tool interfaces by defining strict input preconditions and deterministic error channels.

The bottom layer of @fig-oai-schemas demonstrates the architectural takeaway of this standardized interface. When we adopt language-neutral specifications using Protocol Buffers or JSON-LD, design teams can safely exchange structured attempt traces across organizational boundaries, establishing a shared substrate for pre-trained hardware surrogates without exposing proprietary foundry PDK parameters or confidential RTL code.

## Open PDKs and Cloud Silicon Shuttles {#sec-precompetitive-infrastructure}

Even with standardized data schemas, autonomous exploration loops cannot validate physical feasibility without direct access to silicon signoff targets. Yet when we evaluate physical signoff constraints like wire-delay congestion, power-grid IR drop, UPF power domain boundary isolation, and dynamic thermal throttling, we traditionally encounter expensive commercial EDA licenses and restrictive non-disclosure agreements. As a result, most academic labs and startups cannot test their AI exploration algorithms against realistic physical targets.

We can bridge this divide by expanding open-source physical design infrastructure paired with cloud multi-project wafer shuttle services. Combining open PDKs (such as SkyWater $130\text{ nm}$ or ASAP7 $7\text{ nm}$) and predictive surrogates for leading-edge nodes (such as TSMC N7 and N3) with open EDA frameworks (including OpenROAD, Yosys, OpenSTA, gem5, SCALE-Sim, and Ramulator) creates a fully functional, pre-competitive signoff flow.

This model extends the classic MOSIS fabrication service [@MOSIS1981VLSI] and modern open shuttle aggregators (such as the Google SkyWater Open MPW program and Tiny Tapeout, an accessible open-silicon shuttle initiative) by providing *AI Shuttle Telemetry Grants*. When we give autonomous AI design loops automated paths from AI-generated RTL directly to physical silicon measurements, we close the simulation-to-silicon gap. Standardized containerized environments allow us to evaluate our AI exploration algorithms on realistic physical targets without violating commercial software agreements.

## Consortium Governance and Matched Benchmarks {#sec-neutral-governance}

As open PDKs and cloud shuttles lower the barrier to physical verification, a new challenge emerges. We must ensure that published performance claims reflect genuine microarchitectural breakthroughs rather than benchmark over-optimization or uncalibrated baselines. Without neutral governance standards, our published AI hardware claims easily fall into apples-to-oranges comparisons. Authors select custom benchmarks, keep tuning parameters private, or compare their AI generator against weak baseline heuristics. When we establish multi-stakeholder consortia, we create objective evaluation standards that replace marketing claims with rigorous microarchitectural verification.

Following the governance model established by MLCommons and MLPerf (the open benchmarking suite for machine learning hardware and systems), we should establish an independent Architecture Automation Working Group within established standards bodies (such as MLCommons, SPEC, CHIPS Alliance, or IEEE CEDA). Our working group must enforce three core responsibilities:

* **Defining Reference Problem Suites.** Grounded in realistic industrial constraints, including 3\ W mobile XR spatial processing, RISC-V RV64GCV vector clusters, datacenter tensor acceleration, CXL memory expansion, and UCIe chiplet interconnect management.
* **Structuring Closed and Open Benchmark Divisions.** Establishing a *Closed Division* (where AI agents compete under strictly locked tool wrappers, fixed compute budgets, and identical baseline matching) alongside an *Open Division* (allowing unconstrained search or proprietary surrogates provided authors report multi-dimensional workflow costs).
* **Standardizing Total Workflow Cost Accounting.** Mandating that published benchmarks account for the multi-dimensional resource vector, including GPU compute hours, EDA license checkout minutes, and human triage time.

## Grand Challenges and Architecture Contests {#sec-grand-challenges}

Once neutral governance structures establish rigorous evaluation rules, competitive grand challenges provide the forcing function needed to rally our community around unsolved architectural bottlenecks. Shared competition benchmarks catalyzed autonomous driving through the DARPA Grand Challenges [@BuehlerEtAl2009DARPA; @ThrunEtAl2006Stanley] and computer vision through ImageNet (a large-scale visual recognition benchmark) [@RussakovskyEtAl2015ImageNet]. Annual hardware architecture contests can similarly focus collective engineering effort on high-impact microarchitectural bottlenecks by establishing bold, reproducible milestones.

We should launch three annual competition tracks at top systems and design automation venues (including ISCA, MICRO, HPCA, DAC, ICCAD, and NeurIPS):

1. **Constrained PPA Generation Track.** Generate timing-closed, area-efficient RTL from high-level specifications under strict power and thermal envelopes (such as our Lighthouse 3\ W mobile XR accelerator prompt targeting TSMC N7/N3 nodes from @sec-moonshot and @sec-intent-vs-spec).
2. **Sample-Efficient Space Exploration Track.** Discover Pareto-optimal microarchitectural configurations for heterogeneous workloads (spanning RISC-V RV64GCV vector units and CXL memory topologies) under a strict simulation budget.
3. **Red-Teaming and Hardware Security Track.** Automatically identify latent timing exceptions, prompt-driven Trojan insertions, or verification loopholes in AI-generated hardware collateral using SVA/BMC (SystemVerilog Assertions combined with Bounded Model Checking for formal property verification) with explicit $k$-induction proof depth bounds and invariant coverage guarantees.

## Public Repositories of Failed Attempts {#sec-open-failed-attempts}

While competitive grand challenges highlight successful candidates, the true strength of autonomous search models depends equally on what they learn from failure. Today, our machine learning datasets suffer from severe survivorship bias because they consist almost exclusively of successful, timing-closed designs. As a result, surrogate models trained on these runs fail to recognize physical feasibility boundaries, frequently proposing candidates that violate routing density, AST/CDFG semantics, UPF power domain isolation, or power delivery rules. Public repositories of unroutable placements, negative-slack timing logs, and divergent tool runs supply the negative controls we need to train robust hardware surrogates.

When we create an anonymized, public repository of failed design attempts, we mirror practices in clinical medicine (such as ClinicalTrials.gov, the public registry for clinical research studies requiring negative trial outcome reporting) and aerospace safety (such as NTSB incident databases, the National Transportation Safety Board's accident record system). Learning from unroutable layouts, negative slack reports, and failed synthesis passes enables our AI models to predict physical signoff violations early in the design cycle.

## University Curricula and Conference Badges {#sec-workforce-certification}

Establishing open data contracts, physical signoff harnesses, and failure repositories provides the technical foundation for autonomous design, but infrastructure alone cannot transform an industry. Sustaining Architecture 2.0 at scale ultimately requires a workforce trained to audit, govern, and verify agentic workflows. Preparing our discipline for this responsibility demands that we align university education with peer-reviewed conference badging and enterprise signoff credentials.

Teaching students to manually write HDL code or hand-craft pipeline hazard units as the primary measure of competence is no longer sufficient for an era dominated by autonomous design loops. We must pivot university curricula toward four fundamental areas:

- Formal specification and multi-layer prompt stack engineering.
- Autonomous verification harness design and red-teaming methodologies.
- Evaluator-driven search space formulation and Pareto tradeoff synthesis.
- System integration across CPU, NPU, memory, and packaging boundaries.

To counter Bainbridge's irony of automation [@Bainbridge1983Ironies] and prevent students from becoming moral crumple zones [@Elish2019MoralCrumpleZones], our pedagogy must incorporate diagnostic labs. Students must debug intentionally seeded cross-layer failures in agent-synthesized microarchitectures, building deep physical intuition and diagnostic competence without getting bogged down in routine manual implementation.

In parallel, our conference Artifact Evaluation Committees at venues like ISCA, MICRO, ASPLOS, and DAC should introduce explicit *Autonomous Workflow Certified* (AWC) badges. This badge certifies that an AI architecture study has published complete, reproducible prompt histories, tool execution logs, random seeds, and environmental contracts. Concurrently, we should establish certification standards for *Supported Architecture Claims*. This certification validates that an enterprise architecture team has satisfied all auditability, baseline matching, and failure injection checks before committing a design to expensive silicon tapeout.

## Ecosystem Outlook for Architecture 2.0 at Scale {#sec-ecosystem-outlook}

As university curricula and enterprise badging institutionalize these verification standards across our workforce, closed-loop exploration and agentic tool orchestration can operate at industry scale, driving a profound structural shift in computer architecture. As autonomous workflows absorb routine design mechanics, the fundamental bottlenecks of chip design migrate from manual execution to high-level system formulation, physical signoff governance, and multi-layer constraint trade-offs. This transformation reshapes four critical dimensions of our engineering discipline, spanning architect ownership, EDA industry structures, semiconductor economics, and global chip innovation.

### Architect Ownership and Skill Transformation

As automated design loops absorb the mechanics of RTL coding, physical floorplanning, and standard cell place-and-route sweeps, our primary contribution as architects shifts upstream and downstream. Upstream, we focus on formal problem framing, multi-layer prompt stack specification, objective function synthesis, and safety constraint boundary setting. Downstream, we govern residual risk, evaluate cross-layer tradeoffs, and conduct adversarial red-teaming of AI recommendations.

We become design system architects who engineer both the hardware system and the autonomous loops that build it. We preserve technical contact not by manually editing gates, but by auditing agentic decision traces, inspecting failure counterexamples, and running independent verification checks. Our essential human responsibility remains unchanged. We must declare what the evidence supports, accept residual risk, and recommend commitments to authorized decision makers.

### EDA Industry Structures and Business Models

Beyond the individual architect, scaling autonomous workflows alters the software foundation of our discipline, namely the Electronic Design Automation (EDA) industry. Legacy EDA suites built around monolithic per-seat desktop GUI licenses are giving way to cloud-native, agentic API environments. We repurpose conventional EDA tools (synthesis compilers, static timing analyzers, formal verifiers, physical signoff engines) as headless execution tools and verification oracles within our agentic loops.

Simultaneously, open-source EDA infrastructures (such as OpenROAD, Yosys, OpenSTA, and Verilator) paired with AI search engines achieve parity with proprietary toolchains for a growing spectrum of SoC blocks. EDA business models transition from static per-seat annual licenses to compute-indexed or outcome-contingent pricing, where organizations pay based on design space exploration volume or verified PPA closure milestones.

### Semiconductor Economics and Capital Allocation

As agentic EDA environments compress front-end design cycles from years to weeks, the economic equations governing semiconductor investment undergo a stark realignment. While automated exploration drastically lowers the non-recurring engineering (NRE) labor cost for initial SoC design, it leaves fixed physical capital costs, such as reticle mask sets, foundry shuttle runs, advanced 2.5D/3D packaging dies, and physical silicon validation, unaffected.

Consequently, the economic bottleneck shifts entirely from front-end design labor to back-end physical mask fabrication and packaging yield. This shift triggers a surge in hyper-specialized domain-specific ASICs. Custom chips for micro-verticals (such as edge XR, autonomous robotics, personalized medical devices, and localized AI inference) become economically viable at low production volumes, ending the era of monolithic general-purpose silicon dominance.

### Global Chip Innovation and Ecosystem Dynamics

When transformed pedagogical frameworks, open ISAs (such as RISC-V RV64GCV), open chiplet interconnect standards (such as UCIe), open memory standards (such as CXL), and accessible cloud compute converge, custom silicon creation democratizes worldwide. Hardware startups, regional research centers, and academic laboratories across the globe gain the capability to design competitive, high-performance SoCs previously reserved for mega-cap semiconductor firms.

Furthermore, hardware development cadences align with agile software release cycles. Our silicon architectures iterate on quarterly or monthly schedules using modular chiplet updates and rapid automated design passes, fundamentally accelerating global hardware innovation.

## The Living Architecture 2.0 Web Hub {#sec-living-web-hub}

Accelerating global hardware innovation and supporting agile design cadences cannot occur through static publications or fragmented repositories alone. To translate these macro transformations (alongside the data standards, benchmark suites, and educational frameworks of our roadmap) into daily engineering practice, our community requires a centralized, living infrastructure. Our online companion hub at [arch2.mlsysbook.ai](https://arch2.mlsysbook.ai) serves as this operational nucleus, providing persistent resources for our research, review, and engineering community:

* **The Open Schema and Benchmark Registry.** Machine-readable Protocol Buffer and JSON-LD specifications for design problem formulations, attempt lineage headers, and environmental contracts.
* **The Curated Awesome-Architecture-2.0 Index.** A community-maintained, living directory categorizing papers, datasets, EDA tool wrappers, and AI agent frameworks across all six lifecycle stages.
* **The Interactive Reviewer Audit Tool.** An online checklist implementing the verification rules from @sec-appendix-a-reviewer-checklist, enabling authors and conference reviewers to audit paper rigor prior to submission.
* **Dockerized Reference Starter Kits.** Containerized sandbox environments pre-configured with OpenROAD, Yosys, OpenSTA, gem5, Verilator, SCALE-Sim, Ramulator, UPF tools, and open PDKs (SkyWater $130\text{ nm}$ and ASAP7 $7\text{ nm}$) for immediate experimentation.

## Common Pitfalls {#sec-ecosystem-pitfalls}

Deploying a living web hub and containerized starter kits is only effective if the underlying tools, benchmarks, and training corpora remain active, unbiased, and physically calibrated. Without continuous stewardship and rigorous governance, shared infrastructure quickly degrades into abandoned code or vendor-locked silos. As we operationalize this open ecosystem, we must anticipate and actively mitigate four critical failure modes:

- **Open-source abandonware:** Relying on unmaintained academic scripts, abandoned tool wrappers, or un-versioned container images for core evaluation pipelines. When repository maintainers exit or dependencies shift, research flows break down, rendering published AI hardware benchmarks impossible to replicate.[^fn-abandonware-c12]
- **Proprietary PDK lock-in:** Confining AI design-space exploration algorithms to closed commercial process design kits (PDKs) and proprietary EDA toolchains. Restricting models to non-reproducible, NDA-bound environments prevents open comparison, excludes academic research groups, and restricts cross-organizational transfer.[^fn-pdk-lockin-c12]
- **Uncalibrated contest benchmarks:** Structuring grand challenges or architecture contests around synthetic, easy-to-exploit proxy metrics or uncalibrated test vectors. When competition tasks fail to mirror real-world physical implementation constraints, autonomous agents optimize for benchmark-specific quirks rather than genuine architectural capability.[^fn-contest-benchmarks-c12]
- **Survivorship bias in training corpora:** Training AI surrogates exclusively on successful, timing-closed commercial RTL repositories. Omitting failed synthesis passes, unroutable floorplans, and negative timing slack records leaves models incapable of recognizing physical feasibility boundaries during early exploration.

[^fn-abandonware-c12]: **Bit rot in software infrastructure**: Academic infrastructure decay mirrors open-source software bit rot, where unmaintained repositories rapidly become unusable without active consortium stewardship and containerized CI/CD integration.

[^fn-pdk-lockin-c12]: **Walled gardens in EDA**: NDA-enforced PDK restrictions create a technical walled garden, impeding scientific progress by preventing independent audit and verification of claimed physical design improvements.

[^fn-contest-benchmarks-c12]: **Overfitting in competitive benchmarks**: Uncalibrated contest metrics suffer from the benchmark over-optimization trap observed in machine learning, where systems overfit to specific contest artifacts while degrading on general engineering tasks.

## Open Questions {#sec-ecosystem-open-questions}

Even as our staging sequence establishes open foundations and guards against ecosystem pitfalls, maturing Architecture 2.0 raises fundamental research and policy questions that extend beyond near-term infrastructure bootstrapping. Resolving these open questions requires our community to pursue targeted technical and economic inquiries across three core dimensions:

**EDA tool architectures and agentic infrastructure:** Next-generation tooling must decouple generation from verification while maintaining open evaluation environments.

- **Decoupled execution and verification:** How should next-generation EDA infrastructures decouple generative synthesis agents from formal verification oracles to prevent confirmation bias and agentic hallucination?
- **Open-source evaluator ecosystems:** Can open-source EDA tools provide sufficient fidelity as fast evaluation oracles to drive AI exploration loops without requiring proprietary foundry process design kit (PDK) exposure?

**Semiconductor economics and NRE governance:** Economic feasibility relies on quantitative gatekeeping and clear legal boundaries for generated code.

- **Quantifying NRE ROI gates:** What algorithmic metrics best evaluate whether an AI-proposed microarchitectural optimization justifies the fixed multi-million-dollar NRE mask cost of a leading-edge tapeout?
- **IP provenance and automated indemnification:** What static analysis and provenance-tracing algorithms can guarantee that AI-generated HDL snippets do not infringe on proprietary patent portfolios or violate licensing indemnifications?

**Global chip innovation and agile hardware cadences:** Synchronizing hardware synthesis with rapid software releases demands democratized, versioned benchmarks.

- **Continuous chip integration:** How can hardware organizations synchronize automated silicon synthesis loops with rapid software release cycles without compromising tapeout reliability?
- **Democratized hardware benchmarks:** What versioned benchmark infrastructures (building on the XR Lighthouse Request) can objectively evaluate AI-driven design loops across global research organizations?

## Summary {#sec-ecosystem-coda}

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Build Open Foundations before Scaling Autonomous Tools"}
Scaling Architecture 2.0 across industry and academia requires open data schemas, pre-competitive physical signoff stacks, neutral consortium benchmarks, and public repositories of negative design attempts. We must establish standardized contracts and verification harnesses before deploying autonomous generation tools to ensure that AI-assisted hardware design remains open, auditable, and scientifically reproducible.
:::

Decoupling logic design from physical silicon transformed computer architecture four decades ago by establishing scalable abstraction layers and standard design rules [@MeadConway1980VLSI]. Today, Architecture 2.0 presents an equivalent inflection point. Building an enterprise-grade ecosystem for autonomous hardware exploration requires us to coordinate action across industry, academia, standards bodies, and tooling vendors. We must establish neutral data schemas, open physical signoff stacks, multi-stakeholder consortium benchmarks, and annual grand challenges to transform AI-assisted search from isolated corporate demonstrations into an open, auditable engineering discipline.

As we look to the future of our ecosystem, four core takeaways summarize our roadmap:

- **Staged ecosystem sequence:** We execute ecosystem investments in strict order, establishing foundational data schemas and physical signoff harnesses before deploying autonomous generation tools.
- **Open data contracts:** We standardize open specifications for design problem formulations, attempt lineage headers, and multi-fidelity tool contracts to enable cross-organizational knowledge transfer.
- **Pre-competitive signoff infrastructure:** We combine open PDKs, cloud multi-project wafer shuttles, and containerized EDA toolchains to close the simulation-to-silicon gap for academic and industrial research.
- **Consortium governance and grand challenges:** We establish neutral working groups and annual competition tracks to enforce rigorous baseline comparisons, total workflow cost accounting, and open artifact verification.

The future of hardware design will not be written by locked, black-box generators or proprietary benchmarks. It will be built by an open community of architects, researchers, toolmakers, and domain experts working together to establish verifiable foundations for the next generation of computing. As we step into the era of Architecture 2.0, these shared foundations ensure that artificial intelligence expands our reach while preserving the rigor, auditability, and human accountability that define our discipline.
